title: Preferences for market justice in education: The role of meritocratic beliefs in a comparative perspective
text:
Palabras clave: Market justice preferences; Education; Meritocratic beliefs; Chile; Latent class analysis 

Abstract

title: 2  Introduction
text:
Education has been a central element in the functioning of welfare states by promoting the intellectual and cultural development of individuals, enabling access to opportunities and upward social mobility. However, there are well-documented inequalities within the educational system that highlight how students’ background conditions transform and exacerbate initial inequities. In recent years, the commodification of education has given rise to new forms of inequality, creating a scenario in which the expansion of private education competes with the public sector, and in many cases, the ability to pay is synonymous with access to and quality of education (Busemeyer & Iversen, 2020; Esping-Andersen, 1985; Lindh, 2015; OECD, 2025). This phenomenon becomes particularly concerning when we consider that in countries such as Chile, the United States, or Australia, educational provision is primarily private (Castles et al., 2010; Lee & Stacey, 2024; Valenzuela et al., 2014). These transformations have serious consequences, as market logic and education have come to be viewed as inseparable, leading to the proliferation of various forms of inequality within the education system, such as school segregation and/or the commodification of teaching and learning processes, among others (Piketty & Sandel, 2025).
The processes of commodification, especiallly in education have not only affected institutions but have also had an impact on people’s normative frameworks (Fourcade & Healy, 2007; Koos & Sachweh, 2019). While one might expect most people to support public provision—especially in countries with greater inequality—various studies have shown that segments of the population support the private alternative and may even endorse the inequalities generated by it (Lindh, 2015). This runs counter to general notions of redistribution and social justice, which are rooted in the principles of equality and equity (Walzer, 2010). In this sense, the private architecture of education has been able to reshape people’s sense of justice. Thus, market justice (proposed by Lane (1986)) refers to the view that it is fair for access to and the quality of education to be determined by an individual’s or family’s ability to pay. By viewing money as the guiding principle for the provision of education, this concept addresses the legitimization of inequality, making it essential for understanding the cultural and institutional transformations brought about by the commodification of education.
Meritocracy is a fundamental element of educational institutions, but it has also been viewed as a key factor in legitimizing inequalities. Based on effort and talent, meritocracy posits that these two principles should govern the distribution of rewards in society (Sandel, 2020). However, various studies have shown that meritocratic beliefs are linked to greater acceptance of inequality, as they attribute success and failure primarily to individual responsibility, functioning as a cultural mechanism that justifies social hierarchies and diminishes perceptions of structural factors that shape individual trajectories (Darnon et al., 2018; Heuer et al., 2020; Mau, 2015; Mijs, 2016; Mijs, 2021). In this way, meritocratic beliefs serve as auxiliary frames of reference for all individuals, although they have come to shape a narrative of status legitimation to which those in privileged social positions particularly resort.
Although we know there is a link between meritocracy and the legitimization of inequalities, it is necessary to recognize the different types of meritocratic beliefs held by individuals. Various studies have made progress in unraveling this, offering multidimensional perspectives on meritocracy (Duru-Bellat & Tenret, 2012; Sin et al., 2026; Zhu, 2025). In this context, Castillo et al. (2023) proposes a novel conceptual framework that distinguishes between meritocratic factors—such as effort and talent—and factors of privilege—such as social and economic capital. Furthermore, this framework differentiates between descriptive (perceptions) and ascriptive (preferences) stances, allowing for a better understanding of the multidimensional nature of meritocratic beliefs. However, these meritocratic beliefs take shape and operate differently at the individual and group levels in people’s minds. It is therefore extremely important to account for the heterogeneity and prevalence of each belief configuration observable in society in order to disentangle the web of existing meritocratic belief patterns.
Some studies have sought to understand the diversity of meritocratic beliefs in society (Van Hootegem, 2022; Zhu, 2025), their operationalizations of meritocracy do not distinguish between perceptions and preferences, which has important implications for understanding social reality through measurement. There is also research that has already examined the link between meritocracy and market-oriented preferences but without outlining a typology of beliefs that would allow for a detailed examination of the relationships between these two variables (Castillo et al., 2024; Castillo et al., 2026; Lindh, 2015). In light of the foregoing, we pretend to contribute in this line of research based on two new developments: (1) use the framework of preferences and perceptions proposed by Castillo et al. (2023) to better capture the multidimensional nature of meritocratic beliefs configurations. Later, (2) study the link between of meritocratic beliefs and preferences for market justice in education, aiming to observer in what extent meritocracy works as mechanism of inequalities legitimization.
The study of the relationship between meritocratic beliefs and the legitimization of inequalities is particularly relevant in Chile, a country that has internalized market-based structures into its social services since the military dictatorship, during which education was one of the sectors that underwent extensive privatization—the foundations of which remain in place to this day (Bellei, 2025; Valenzuela et al., 2014). Furthermore, the country’s high levels of inequality are striking given its population’s strong adherence to meritocracy, especially with regard to the value placed on effort (Castillo et al., 2025). Thus, this study aims to contribute to the research on legitimization of inequalities based on two questions: (1) To what extent do meritocratic beliefs influence preferences for market justice in education? (2) How do institutional designs and preferences for market justice in education interact?. This will be answered by analyzing how different configurations of meritocratic beliefs are associated with market justice preferences in education through Latent Class Analysis (LCA). More specifically, we seek to provide a detailed understanding of how the interaction of individual variables can explain the justification of inequality in education. Thus, this research advances our understanding of how people’s normative judgments regarding the legitimization of inequality in education vary, elucidating the factors that shape them. This can provide an assessment of how people normatively perceive the functioning of education, which may serve as a basis for the development of policies aimed at promoting educational justice.
To adress these issues, we use representative data from the chilean survey EDUMERCO, a study fielded at 2025 to examine attitudes, emotions, and behaviors among adults aged 18 to 75 in relation to inequalities and meritocracy. First, we applied latent class analysis to identify configurations of meritocratic beliefs, and then conduct multinomial logistic regression to examine the relationship between these profiles and preferences for market justice in education, while incorporating sociodemographic and institutional factors.

title: 3  Theoretical and empirical background
text:
3.1 Market justice preferences
Welfare states have undergone several institutional transformations in recent years, with private expansion strongly penetrating the field of social services alongside public provision (Busemeyer & Iversen, 2020). Such processes have led to changes in the architecture of the institutions responsible for social welfare. On the one hand, private companies operate as service administrators of benefits based on the user’s ability to pay, whereas on the other hand, public providers have reorganized to compete as quasi-markets (Lindh, 2017). Besides changes at the formal level, the commodification of social services shapes cultural norms and beliefs, where markets operate as moral projects (Fourcade & Healy, 2007; Koos & Sachweh, 2019).
The field of distributive justice has gradually incorporated market preferences into attitudinal research on redistribution. Since Kluegel’s seminal work (1981) on the normative foundations of beliefs about social stratification, the concept of market justice preferences has been developed, understood as the normative principle that legitimizes access to goods and services according to an individual’s or family’s ability to pay (Lane, 1986). This principle is closely linked to the justification of inequalities: by conceiving the market as a space of equal opportunities, economic success is interpreted as an individual achievement (J. R. Kluegel et al., 1999), disregarding the structural conditions that produce such disparities. In this way, market justice operates simultaneously as an economic and moral principle that legitimizes socioeconomic inequalities.
Most research in this field relies on survey data, in which questions about market justice directly probe support for the provision of social services—education, pensions, and health care—based on individual ability to pay (e.g., “Is it fair that high-income individuals receive better education than low-income individuals?”) (Busemeyer, 2013; Lindh, 2015). Within this framework, ISSP has been the primary source for advancing this agenda. Also, recent research has employed both indices constructed from relevant items (Castillo, Laffert, et al., 2025) and a separate analysis of each item.
Education is one of the key dimensions in the study of market justice, given the commodification processes educational systems have undergone in recent decades. The growing prominence of the private sector in education, coupled with the implementation of market-driven logic, has transformed the structure of educational systems, where students and their families are viewed as consumers of a service (Brancaleone & O’Brien, 2011; Lindh, 2015). These changes have ethical consequences, as education loses its intrinsic value and becomes a means of generating monetary value, and its quality is often determined by the type of funding, thereby reinforcing socioeconomic inequalities (Abowitz & Stitzlein, 2018; Ball, 2004; Piketty & Sandel, 2025; Satz, 2010). In this sense, market justice in education conflicts with educational justice by denying equity in quality and universal access to education.
Recent literature on market preferences has identified significant associations at both the individual and contextual levels. At the individual level, socioeconomic status emerges as a consistent predictor; those in more advantaged positions tend to exhibit greater preferences for market justice (Koos & Sachweh, 2019; Lindh, 2015), a pattern reflecting a moral economy oriented toward justifying status for those who benefit from the market order. In this regard, political ideology shows a clear association, with right-leaning individuals tending to favor market-oriented distributional principles (Castillo et al., 2024; Lee & Stacey, 2024). At the contextual level, the relative weight of private and public service provision emerges as a structuring factor in preferences; in countries where private investment predominates, individuals tend to internalize the market order as a criterion of justice and, consequently, to reduce their redistributive preferences; whereas the opposite trend is observed where public provision prevails (Busemeyer, 2013; Immergut & Schneider, 2020; Lindh, 2015).

title: 3  Theoretical and empirical background
text:
3.3 Education and class
There are various theories regarding how educational attainment affects people’s redistributive preferences. On the one hand, there are theories that view education as a source of resources that enhances the development of technical skills and/or critical thinking, leading individuals to become aware of structural problems and, as a result, to support the reduction of inequality (Becker, 1993; Freire, 2015; Schultz, 1961). On the other hand, in cultural reproduction theories, education has been understood as a source of social inequalities, as it reproduces individuals’ living conditions, preventing opportunities for intergenerational social mobility and, consequently, perpetuating the stratified social order (Bourdieu, 2019; Bowles & Gintis, 2011). Within the framework of redistributive preferences, reproductionist notions are grounded in self-interest theory, whereby those with higher levels of education tend to exhibit attitudes that reflect a desire to protect their privileged social positions—which, in terms of attitudes, could be understood as an aversion to redistribution or support for market-based justice. Thus, education can be understood not only through its enlightening role in social life but also as a cog in the reproduction of inequalities in society.
Recent literature provides empirical support for these two theoretical approaches to education. For example, research by Nye et al. (2026) found, in an analysis of 282 country-year combinations from various international surveys, that in 95% of cases, education was positively associated with market-oriented attitudes. Likewise, Van Noord et al. (2019) used data from 31 countries to show that education is widely understood as the basis for social stratification. Other studies have found that higher levels of education are associated with a greater preference for public investment (Busemeyer, 2012) However, the results from Liu & Wang (2026) suggest that education does not fulfill a generalized function; rather, both the enlightening and the reproductionist roles exist but depend on the level of education, where in countries with low inequality, basic education is associated with reproductionist positions, while in secondary and tertiary education, the enlightening role stands out.
Given the important role that education plays in shaping individuals’ attitudes toward inequality, this study proposes the following hypothesis:
\(H_{2}\): Higher levels of education will be negatively associated with a preference for market-based justice in education.
In addition to educational level, the literature has shown that social class is also an important factor in the study of attitudes toward inequality (Kulin & Svallfors, 2013; Lindh, 2015; Lindh & McCall, 2020). The evidence shows that higher social classes tend to support market-based distributive principles (Immergut & Schneider, 2020; Lindh, 2015). In this context, among higher-income social groups, there is a congruence between their attitudes and their individual outcomes—that is, a legitimization of the market as a distributor of rewards that serves as a justification for social status. However, Langsæther & Evans (2020) emphasizes the complexity of attitude formation beyond a mere expression of self-interest and points to the case of the self-employed, whose income and social security are similar to those of the working class but who share preferences with the upper classes. Based on the literature, the corresponding hypothesis is:
\(H_{3}\): Individuals from higher social classes are more likely to prefer market-based justice in education
This study aims to contribute to the research on multidimensional meritocracy but in a novel way: by analyzing how different configurations of meritocratic beliefs are associated with market justice preferences in education. More specifically, we seek to provide a detailed understanding of how the interaction of individual and contextual variables can explain the justification of inequality in education differently depending on the country. Thus, this research advances our understanding of how people’s normative judgments regarding the legitimization of inequality in education vary, elucidating the factors that shape them. This can provide an assessment of how people normatively perceive the functioning of education, which may serve as a basis for the development of policies aimed at promoting educational justice.

title: 3  Theoretical and empirical background
text:
3.2 Meritocratic beliefs
When discussing education, it is difficult not to encounter the concept of meritocracy. Based on Michael Young’s work The Rise of Meritocracy (1962) (2017), this concept is understood as the distribution of rewards based on effort and talent. For their part, schools operate by awarding credentials that reflect students’ performance in various subjects. In this sense, meritocracy is a fundamental element of every educational institution, as it is one of the principles governing the awarding of credentials. Thus, beliefs about the educational system are often closely tied to meritocracy (Clycq et al., 2014; Darnon et al., 2018).
In the field of education, meritocracy has been used as a distributive principle, but within this framework it has also been linked to the justification of inequalities. Starting from Adams’ theory of equity (1963), meritocracy operates as a universal equality principle, where rewards should be commensurate with effort. Several studies have shown that meritocratic beliefs are associated with individualistic beliefs such as an aversion to redistribution and a preference for market justice (Bartram, 2023; Castillo et al., 2024; Castillo, Iturra, et al., 2025; Mijs, 2021; Sin et al., 2026), and are a characteristic value of those in more privileged social positions (Heuer et al., 2020). In these cases, meritocracy is used as a means of legitimizing positions, where those who enjoy the benefits of the system tend to justify their success on the basis of their own merit, overlooking the structural conditions that shape reality. Thus, the narrative of merit is used to support the idea that money should determine the quality of and access to education. This normative judgment runs counter to educational justice, as it hinders equal opportunities and, ultimately, determines students’ educational trajectories (Moyano, 2020; Walzer, 2010).
In the meritocracy research framework, most studies have been based on survey items where International Social Survey Program emerges as the main instrument to measure and analise meritocratic beliefs both nacional and internacional contexts. This items show the relevance of meritocratic and priviliege factors for getting ahead in life like the effort and the contacts respectively. Following this conceptual model, there is a tradition of studying meritocratic beliefs from a unidimensional perspective (García-Sánchez et al., 2019; Mijs, 2021). The fundamental assumption of this perspective is that the factors are negatively correlated; for example, if one expresses a higher degree of meritocratic beliefs, consequently, beliefs that account for structural factors decrease. The problem with this approach is that it has serious implications for understanding social reality, since people’s beliefs cannot be assumed to follow a rational logic where, if one goes up, the other must go down. To address this, in recent years several authors have proposed a multidimensional perspective on meritocracy, constructing frameworks that allow for distinguishing the dimension of merit from that of privilege, on the one hand, and differentiating perceptions from preferences on the other (Castillo et al., 2023; Duru-Bellat & Tenret, 2012; Zhu, 2025). These advances have led to two key contributions: to capture the coexistence of beliefs that may be considered contradictory to reflect the coexistence of beliefs that may be considered contradictory (1) and, consequently, to demonstrate that people can hold different sets of meritocratic beliefs (2).
While the multidimensional perspective of meritocracy allows for a more detailed examination of people’s beliefs, a caveat remains regarding the individuals who hold those beliefs. The literature has shown a prevalence of variable-centered methods—that is, methods that identify an association between two or more variables in a general population, assuming that such an association is uniform across individuals (Cech & Blair-Loy, 2010). Following this approach, it is not possible to determine whether there are different configurations of people’s beliefs and what factors influence this differentiation. Given these limitations, latent class analysis (LCA) is a novel, person-centered method that allows us to identify the heterogeneity of individuals’ beliefs based on their clustering. One of the advantages of this approach is that it accommodates the possibility that individuals may hold both meritocratic and structuralist beliefs, allowing for a theoretical and methodological examination of multidimensional meritocracy (Nylund-Gibson & Choi, 2018; Zhu, 2025). By identifying latent groups, LCA enables the observation of qualitative typological variations, which in turn facilitates a detailed examination of how contextual variables interact with individual variables to shape people’s meritocratic beliefs.
Although LCA is not a widely used method in sociological studies, some research has demonstrated its effectiveness in identifying heterogeneous groups and the variations that persist across countries (Van Hootegem, 2022). Zhu (2025) presented how meritocratic beliefs vary in the United States, Finland, and China, where three types of latent groups were identified: those with purely meritocratic beliefs, predominantly meritocratic beliefs, and dual consciousness. Therefore, based on previous studies, this research hypothesizes three types of groups based on meritocratic beliefs:
\(H_{1}\): (1) purely meritocratic beliefs, viewing merits as important while deeming structural factors as irrelevant; (2) purely structuralist beliefs, viewing structural factors as important while deeming merits as unimportant; (3) dual consciousness, viewing merits and structural factors as important simultaneously.
